title: Knee Pain When Climbing Stairs: Why It Happens and What Helps
metaDescription: Knee pain on stairs is often early knee arthritis or weak thigh muscles. Learn the causes, simple exercises, and when to see an orthopaedic doctor.
intro: Pain on stairs is one of the most common early signs of knee arthritis. Stairs put more strain on the knee than walking on flat ground, so a tired or worn knee complains first. The good news is that most people improve with simple treatment, stronger thigh muscles and a little patience.

sections.heading: Why does my knee hurt on stairs?
sections.body: The most common reason in people over 45 is knee arthritis, where the cushion inside the joint has become rough and thin. Weak thigh muscles, an old injury, extra body weight, or a problem under the kneecap can also cause it. An examination tells us which one applies to you.

sections.heading: Is stair pain always arthritis?
sections.body: No. Arthritis is common, but pain on stairs can also come from the kneecap, a torn cartilage pad (meniscus), or a tendon around the knee. Pain with locking, catching, or sudden swelling after a twist points more to an injury and should be checked.

sections.heading: What helps right now?
sections.body: Start with the simple things. Hold the handrail, take one step at a time, and avoid carrying heavy loads up stairs. A painkiller gel on the knee can help, and tablets if your doctor advises them. Resting completely makes the knee stiffer, so keep gently moving.

sections.heading: Which exercises make stairs easier?
sections.body: Strong thigh muscles take pressure off the knee. Versus Arthritis suggests simple exercises such as sit-to-stand from a chair, step-ups on a low step, and straight-leg raises. Start gently and build up slowly. They work best once your pain has settled a little with medicines.
bullets: Sit-to-stand: stand up from a firm chair and sit down slowly.
Step-ups: step up and down on one low step, holding a rail.
Straight-leg raises: lie down and lift your straight leg a short way.

sections.heading: Does losing weight help my knees on stairs?
sections.body: Yes. Being at a healthy weight reduces the pressure on your knees with every step. The NHS and Versus Arthritis both advise weight loss if you are overweight, and even a modest loss helps.

sections.heading: When should I stop managing it myself?
sections.body: See a doctor if stair pain lasts more than a few weeks, keeps you from going out, wakes you at night, or comes with swelling or giving way. We usually go step by step: medicines first, then exercises, then physiotherapy treatments, then an injection, and surgery only if it suits you.

faqs.q: Should I avoid stairs if I have knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Not completely. Use the stairs when you need to, hold the rail, and go slowly. Avoiding all movement makes the knee stiffer.

faqs.q: Can knee pain on stairs go away?
faqs.a: Often it improves a lot with medicines, exercises and weight control, though arthritis itself does not disappear.

faqs.q: Is knee pain on stairs a sign I need a knee replacement?
faqs.a: Not by itself. Replacement is considered only if pain still limits your life after other treatment has been tried.

faqs.q: Is cycling good for knee pain on stairs?
faqs.a: Cycling and swimming are low-impact ways to build leg strength, according to Versus Arthritis.

faqs.q: Should I get an X-ray for stair pain?
faqs.a: If it lasts more than a few weeks, an examination and sometimes an X-ray help your doctor find the cause.
